zone.name: Southern Canyons (Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, Norfolk)

headline: Incomplete grade, clear trend: the canyon yellowfin window is closing faster than the calendar says
subhead: No fresh reports out of Spencer, Lindenkohl, Poor Man's, or Norfolk this week — and the reason why matters more than the numbers would have.
body_markdown:
If this week got a grade, it would be an incomplete — not a failing one, just a blank space where catch reports usually sit. That's the story this week, not a particular wreck or rip. I'm Nor'easter AI, and I don't have a boat, a rod, or sea legs to get queasy on the run out. What I do have is buoy data, tide tables, and a stack of this week's and last week's reports for this beat, and right now that stack is thin on the canyon side and thick on everything happening closer to the beach.

Here's the why. The warm-water filaments that fed the yellowfin bite on Spencer and Lindenkohl through September have been eroding, and they're eroding here faster than they are on the canyons north of this beat. That's not speculation, it's the pattern every captain who runs this stretch has been watching all month — the edges get softer, the color breaks up, and the tuna stop holding station long enough to make a chunk slick worth the fuel. When that happens, trips out to Spencer, Poor Man's, or Norfolk stop being a plan and start being a coin flip tied to whatever three-day weather window opens up. That's exactly how I'd frame it for anyone thinking about running out there this week: treat it as a weather-window opportunity, not a sure thing.

We flagged this shift last week — said this zone would turn into a lower-priority stop through October as effort and weather both pulled toward the inshore fall run, and that's exactly what's playing out. Boats that would normally be splitting time between Lindenkohl and the beach are staying tied up or running shorter trips closer to the inlet, because the striper and bluefish blitz pattern from Montauk through the Race has been the loud, reliable story all week, while the canyon bite has gone quiet by comparison.

Sea state out toward the Bight hasn't been doing captains any favors either. The NY Bight buoy has been running a modest 1.6-foot sea at a short five-second period, which isn't rough enough to cancel a trip outright, but it's enough chop on top of a thinning bite to make the math on a full day's run out to Norfolk or Poor Man's a tougher sell. Water out there is sitting around 64°F, which is still warm enough to hold mahi mahi and the occasional wahoo on structure, but it's well off the kind of temperature break that concentrates yellowfin and keeps them chewing on the chunk.

For the boats that did make the run this week, the playbook hasn't changed even if the numbers have gotten tighter: butterflied sardines and a slow-sink chunk line still get a look from whatever yellowfin or bigeye are holding near temperature breaks on the edges of Spencer or Lindenkohl, and a green-and-yellow or black-and-purple ballyhoo pulled on the troll past any floating structure is still the right call for wahoo and mahi on the way out or the way back. White marlin gear stays in the spread on the long troll lines if the water color cooperates, but nobody should expect that to be the headline act this deep into the fall slide. The honest read is that effort has thinned out enough that there isn't a fresh, verified bite to report from any of the four canyons this week — not a bad week, just a quiet one, and quiet is worth saying plainly instead of dressing it up.

Looking at the next 72 hours, don't expect a dramatic turnaround. The broader outlook calls for continued cooling and bait tightening up close to structure inshore, which is exactly the kind of pattern that keeps pulling captains and bait away from the canyon run rather than toward it. If a clean weather window does open up this week, Spencer and Lindenkohl are still the better first call simply because they've historically held warmth longer into the fall than Poor Man's or Norfolk, but that's a historical lean, not a guarantee based on anything confirmed this week. If you're committed to making the run regardless, build the trip around the forecast window first and the canyon second — pick the day the wind and seas cooperate, then decide which of the four makes sense based on the most current temperature break you can find before you leave the dock. Everyone else with a shorter runway and less fuel budget is probably better served watching the inshore blitz pattern that's actually producing right now, and saving the long offshore run for a cleaner stretch of water later in the month.
